preamble: Shift of the palatalized alveolar stop [tʲ] to the palatal stop [c], with the secondary palatal articulation becoming the primary place. In Old Czech, the main depalatalization (13th–14th centuries) either merged soft consonants with their hard counterparts or turned them into the palatals ť, ď, ň; before i and ě the soft t became [c]. Slovak shows the same development before e and i, where Czech instead depalatalized t before e (Czech teplý [ˈtɛpliː] vs Slovak teplý [ˈcepliː]).

examples.from: Old Czech soft t’ in tělo 'body' (Proto-Slavic *tělo)
examples.note: Palatalized t’ became the palatal stop ť [c], spelled t before ě and i.
Czech has hard t here: teplý [ˈtɛpliː].
